sources.title: National Ainu Museum: permanent exhibition, from Ainu perspectives
sources.note: Direct official page read. Earlier archivenam.ainu-upopoy.jp/en/exhibition/floor2/basic/ contains the same exhibition text; treat as one work for reuse. Overview describes indigenous communities and regional history, not one centralized state. Map dates and bounds are independently decoded in identities.json.

sources.title: Foundation for Ainu Culture: History and Culture of the Ainu People, August 2026
sources.note: Direct PDF text read. Printed pages 2 to 6, PDF pages 4 to 8: formation, excavated ikupasuy, 1604 trade grant and 1669 war. All chapters share one 200-word budget. Older rekishi_bunka_english.pdf is substantially the same work and must be aggregated for reuse. Regional formation dates are debated.

sources.title: Hokkaido Digital Museum: Okhotsk and Satsumon cultures
sources.note: Direct prefectural museum synthesis read: Okhotsk culture; Satsumon culture; Meeting between northern and southern cultures. Archaeological cultures are not automatically ethnic identities. Avoid treating accumulated dwelling counts as a contemporary population.

sources.title: Suzuki Takuya, Hokkaido Museum: A koshiki steamer and food culture 1,300 years ago
sources.note: Japanese curatorial article, reprinted from the spring 2021 museum newsletter. Direct read. Yura site excavation in 1959; eighth-century Satsumon pottery steamer, object 131775. Article gives operation, holes, grain and cloth. Exact grain species in this vessel is not established.

sources.title: Hokkaido Government Red Brick exhibition: fourteenth to sixteenth centuries
sources.note: Direct official text read: changes in cookware and dwellings; Wajin trading settlements and tate. Other sections of this exhibition are conservatively aggregated in work-budget-checks.json.

sources.title: Hokkaido Government Red Brick exhibition: Ainu people and the Matsumae domain
sources.note: Direct public HTML downloaded and read; witness matsumae.html. Salmon and pelts exchanged for rice, sake and iron; domain economy depended on trade, unfair practices and Shakushain resistance. Exact 1669 date is cited to the Foundation booklet separately.

sources.title: Hokkaido Government Red Brick exhibition: 1869 to 1945
sources.note: Direct official text read. Renaming and development in 1869, restrictions on language, customs and livelihoods, land loss. Later context explicitly outside the imported map interval. Do not infer that every forced relocation occurred in 1875.

sources.title: University of Tokyo Tokoro Research Laboratory: outline of Tokoro-chashi sites
sources.note: Direct university archaeological archive read. Terrace near river mouth, several distinct site concentrations, Initial Jomon through Ainu remains; chashi approximately early eighteenth century, separate older Okhotsk pit houses; investigations from 1960. The fort date is approximate, not a precise 1700 event.

sources.title: Hokkaido Digital Museum: traditional food, clothing and housing
sources.note: Direct read. Page explicitly concerns ways of life 100 to 200 years ago, rather than all periods. Fish skin clothes; daily meals and preservation; dwelling interior; surroundings and household waste. No toilet or sewer claim is supported by the waste passage.

sources.title: Hokkaido Museum: the culture and recent history of the Ainu
sources.note: Direct collection interpretation read: Saranip, Dwelling restored with Yaichiro Hama, Ainu Language Blocks, and poster for Ainu youth speeches around 1930. Contemporary teaching blocks are not evidence for historical schools.

sources.title: Hokkaido Digital Museum: literature orally passed from person to person
sources.note: Direct text read: heroic/mythic epics and prose tales; thirteen Ainu and Japanese narratives published in 1923 by Chiri Yukie, who lived 1903 to 1922. Avoid broader first-ever-writing claim.

sources.title: Chiri Yukie: Ainu Shin’yoshu, 1923, Aozora Bunko transcription
sources.note: Direct primary text read. Preface dated March 1, 1922; contents and first tale have Shirokanipe ranran pishkan, paired with Japanese 銀の滴降る降るまわりに. English translation here is a concise rendering of that Japanese. Original published Roman spelling retained. Three Ainu words plus five English translation words total eight quoted/translated lyric words. Aozora base edition is Iwanami 1978, digitizing the 1923 work.

sources.title: Upopoy National Ainu Museum and Park: Ainu culture and language
sources.note: Direct official page read. Ainu is distinct from Japanese, historically spoken and later transcribed using Latin and katakana; modern transmission of dance, music, woodcarving and embroidery. No claim of an ancient local alphabet.

batchIdentityNotes.decision: Share one explicitly phased cultural card, preserving three distinct imported intervals; no centralized kingdom or ancient founding claim.
batchIdentityNotes.geometry: Decoded 34 Historical Basemaps features. Early ainu polygons extend to approximately 34.88 degrees N in Honshu. Most later outlines combine Hokkaido, Sakhalin and the Kurils; some late outlines omit southern portions of Hokkaido. These are coarse imported cultural extents, not modern sovereignty boundaries.
batchIdentityNotes.historicalCaveat: The -4000 beginning conflates earlier regional archaeology and later Ainu identity. Formation is usually associated with the twelfth to thirteenth centuries and varied regionally. Early phase boundaries are interpretive approximate divisions, not accessions.
batchIdentityNotes.laterEvidence: Household accounts are explicitly nineteenth- and early twentieth-century context; Hama reconstruction, Chiri writing, youth speeches and language blocks are expressly dated or described as modern. No ancient script, toilet system, medical treatment or formal ancient school is invented.
